item.title: SMHIGridClim, 2.5 km resolution gridded climatology of Fennoscandia
item.description:
SMHIGridClim, 2.5 km resolution gridded climatology of Fennoscandia
Sandra Andersson, Maria Norman, Tomas Landelius, Patrick Samuelsson, Semjon Schimanke, Maida Zahid, and Lars Bärring
Earth Syst. Sci. Data, 18, 8569–8589, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8569-2026, 2026
This study introduces SMHIGridClim (Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute Gridded Climatology), a high-resolution gridded climatology for Fennoscandia, covering the period from 1961 to 2018. It provides detailed climate data, including temperature, humidity, precipitation, and snow depth at a 2.5 km resolution. The dataset is created by combining observations from multiple meteorological institutes with reanalysis data. The study highlights the benefits of SMHIGridClim, making it a valuable resource for climate research in the Nordic region.

item.title: SISAL_monv1: a global database of cave monitoring observations
item.description:
SISAL_monv1: a global database of cave monitoring observations
Pauline C. Treble, Yining Zang, Nikita Kaushal, István G. Hatvani, Péter Tanos, Zoltan Kern, Andy Baker, Andreas Hartmann, Franziska A. Lechleitner, Bryce Belanger, Bruna Daudt de Oliveira, Will Sinclair, Dana F. C. Riechelmann, András Hidas, Kei Yoshimura, Laia Comas-Bru, and SISAL working group members
Earth Syst. Sci. Data, 18, 8667–8691, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8667-2026, 2026
Water dripping from cave ceilings is studied to understand how water moves from the surface to the cave. This has applications for palaeoclimate, groundwater and cave conservation studies. We present a new database containing water isotope measurements for drip water and rainfall at 75 cave locations globally. The database is a SISAL working group initiative (Speleothem Isotopes Synthesis and AnaLysis) and complements cave speleothem databases previously constructed by SISAL.

item.title: The ICOS Ecosystem Station Loobos: a pine forest site exposed to atmospheric pollution
item.description:
The ICOS Ecosystem Station Loobos: a pine forest site exposed to atmospheric pollution
Michiel K. van der Molen, Henk Snellen, Rupert Holzinger, Johannes G. M. Barten, Hong Zhao, Laurens Ganzeveld, Julie Fry, Wouter Peters, Maarten Krol, Jordi Vila-Guerau de Arrellano, and Bart Kruijt
Earth Syst. Sci. Data, 18, 8637–8666, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8637-2026, 2026
In 2021, a second tower was built in Loobos (NL-Loo) to measure carbon dioxide and water fluxes, as an Integrated Carbon Observing System (ICOS) Class 2 Ecosystem station. Extra instruments were installed to measure VOC and ozone fluxes. This paper describes the site’s geological and cultural history, ecosystem composition, instrumentation and ancillary ecosystem measurements. The paper goes into the quality of the measurements and continuity with respect to the first tower.

item.title: A multi-decadal dataset of surface damage on Antarctic ice shelves (1999–2024)
item.description:
A multi-decadal dataset of surface damage on Antarctic ice shelves (1999–2024)
Leyue Tang, Jonathan L. Bamber, Tian Li, and Gang Qiao
Earth Syst. Sci. Data, 18, 8591–8615, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8591-2026, 2026
Many Antarctic ice shelves are thinning and retreating, threatening future sea-level rise. Surface damage indicates structural weakening, but long-term records are scarce. We created a multi-decadal surface damage record for nine representative Antarctic ice shelves using satellite imagery and deep learning. Among them, Pine Island, Thwaites and Scar Inlet have experienced the most significant changes in surface damage during the study period, providing insights into ice shelf stability.

item.title: 4D Aviation Emission Inventory Data of China estimated with QAR data in 2023 (4D-AEID-2023)
item.description:
4D Aviation Emission Inventory Data of China estimated with QAR data in 2023 (4D-AEID-2023)
Binbin Lu, Lingkun Shi, Chun Wang, Huabo Sun, Qinli Guo, Xinbo Wang, and Xuhui Wang
Earth Syst. Sci. Data, 18, 8617–8636, https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-18-8617-2026, 2026
Airplane emissions are usually estimated, not measured. We used flight data recorders from 4.52 million Chinese flights in 2023 to track real fuel burn and pollution, second by second. Aviation in China burned 23.7 million tonnes of fuel, emitting 74.6 million tonnes of CO2 unevenly: just 10 % of flight paths produce 74 % of emissions, and brief ground idling causes disproportionate pollution. This precise data helps target routes and airport operations where emission cuts matter most.

item.title: Auditing the Global Carbon Budget: exploring the 2024–2025 vintage shift
item.description:
Auditing the Global Carbon Budget: exploring the 2024–2025 vintage shift
Mikkel Bennedsen, Eric Hillebrand, and Siem Jan Koopman
Earth Syst. Sci. Data Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-2026-905,2026
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments)
Every year, the Global Carbon Budget reports how much carbon dioxide human activities release and how much ends up in the atmosphere, on land, and in the ocean. These widely used accounts never balance exactly, but for years the gap averaged out to nearly zero. We built statistical checks that trace such gaps to their sources and find that revisions in the 2025 edition leave a gap that no longer averages away. Anyone combining numbers from different editions should take this into account.

item.title: Development of an integrated source-profile dataset of high reactivity organic gases (HROG) for anthropogenic sources in China
item.description:
Development of an integrated source-profile dataset of high reactivity organic gases (HROG) for anthropogenic sources in China
Yaqin Gao, Hongli Wang, Rusha Yan, Sheng'ao Jing, Qian Wang, Jun Lu, Jingyu An, Yuhang Wu, Xinwei Feng, Yingge Ma, Dan Dan Huang, Yingjie Li, Haixia Dai, Qingyan Fu, and Cheng Huang
Earth Syst. Sci. Data Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-2026-927,2026
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments)
Organic gases from industry, coatings, vehicles, evaporation and residential combustion drive ozone formation, yet many remain missing. We tested real sources and built emission fingerprints for five source types. Previously overlooked gases, notably oxygen- and nitrogen-containing ones, often dominate their chemical reactivity. Air quality models using our fingerprints simulate pollution more accurately, helping regulators curb the most reactive gases, not just the largest emission amounts.
